processing: Mostly green tea; the best-known modern product, Zhaopo Lüjian, is pan-fired from single early-spring buds into a flat shape. Black tea is also made under the name.
harvest_season: Early spring; Zhaopo Lüjian uses single buds picked before Qingming.
appearance_dry: For Zhaopo Lüjian, flat, even buds of a glossy tender green.
taste_profile: Fresh, mellow and sweet-finishing with a clear, lasting fragrance, based on descriptions of Zhaopo Lüjian.

brewing.notes: General guidance for flat bud greens: cool water and a glass or open gaiwan, with no lid left on between steeps.

vintage_note: The green tea is sold as a current-year spring harvest, with pre-Qingming bud tea at the top. As usual for greens it is best within the year. Zhaopo Lüjian, on the market since 2002, is a brand product within the wider regional name, so check which you are buying.
description:
Zhaopo Tea comes from Mianzhu in northern Sichuan, on the edge of the Chengdu Plain. Local pride ranks it with the area's woodblock New Year prints and Jiannanchun liquor, and it is both a historic name and a modern protected product.

Green tea is the core, though black tea is also made under the name. The modern flagship, Zhaopo Lüjian, is pan-fired from single early-spring buds into a flat, even shape, which is said to follow the older methods.

The flagship is described as fresh and mellow with a clear fragrance and a sweet finish, and it brews to an apricot-green liquor. Treat it like other flat bud greens, with cool water and short steeps.

When buying, separate the regional name from the brand. Zhaopo Lüjian belongs to one company, while Zhaopo Tea is the wider name. Tribute claims appear on nearly every package, so go by the date and the leaf instead.
history:
Zhaopo is usually described as a tribute tea of the Tang, a claim mostly carried by regional and promotional writing. A firmer literary trace is a line by the Southern Song poet Lu You comparing a tasting of Zhaopo to splashing milk. The name also appears in a Chinese tea dictionary, ranked with Emei and Mengding teas.

The modern product line took shape later. Zhaopo Lüjian came to market in 2002, and Zhaopo tea is now listed as a Chinese geographical-indication product.
